input.candidate_text:
Assume for contradiction that \(x>1\).

For every odd prime \(p\mid y\) with \(p\nmid x\), let \(\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\) denote the multiplicative order of \(x\pmod p\). Let \(L\) be the least common multiple of these orders, taking \(L=1\) if there are no such primes.

Choose an odd prime \(\ell\nmid x^{2L}+1\), and put \(k=\ell L\) and \(N=x^{2k}+1\). Define
\[
e=\begin{cases}2,&2\mid y\text{ and }x\text{ is odd},\\1,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
\qquad Q=\frac{N}{e}.
\]
We claim that \(\gcd(Q,xy)=1\). Certainly \(\gcd(N,x)=1\). If an odd prime \(p\mid y\) also divides \(x\), then \(N\equiv1\pmod p\). If \(p\mid y\) but \(p\nmid x\), then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\mid L\), so
\[
x^{2k}=x^{2\ell L}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and hence \(N\equiv2\pmod p\). Thus no odd prime divisor of \(y\) divides \(N\). If \(x\) is odd, then \(N\equiv2\pmod8\), so dividing by \(e\) removes the only possible common factor \(2\). This proves the claim.

Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{ord}_Q(x)=4k.
\]
Indeed, \(x^{2k}\equiv-1\pmod Q\), so the order divides \(4k\) but is not a divisor of \(2k\). If it were a proper divisor of \(4k\), it would be less than \(2k\); say it were \(d<2k\). Then \(Q\mid x^d-1\), whereas
\[
0<x^d-1\le x^{2k-1}-1<\frac{x^{2k}+1}{2}\le Q,
\]
a contradiction.

By Fermat's congruence \(x^\ell\equiv x\pmod\ell\),
\[
N=x^{2\ell L}+1\equiv x^{2L}+1\not\equiv0\pmod\ell.
\]
Hence \(\gcd(\ell,Q)=1\).

Because \(y\) is invertible modulo \(Q\), choose \(a\) satisfying
\[
ay\equiv x^k\pmod Q.
\]
By the Chinese remainder theorem, there is a residue class \(c\pmod{\ell Q}\) satisfying
\[
c\equiv a\pmod Q,\qquad c\equiv2\pmod\ell.
\]
It is coprime to \(\ell Q\). By Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, choose a prime \(r\equiv c\pmod{\ell Q}\).

Then
\[
ry\equiv x^k\pmod Q,
\]
so \((ry)^2\equiv x^{2k}\equiv-1\pmod Q\). Therefore
\[
Q\mid (ry)^2+1.
\]
Applying the hypothesis with \(n=r\), and using \(\varphi(r)=r-1\), gives
\[
Q\mid x^{r-1}-1.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{ord}_Q(x)=4k\), we obtain \(4k\mid r-1\), and in particular \(\ell\mid r-1\). But \(r\equiv2\pmod\ell\), so \(r-1\equiv1\pmod\ell\), a contradiction.

Thus \(x>1\) is impossible. Since \(x\) is a positive integer, necessarily \(x=1\).

problem.theorem:
Let \( x \) and \( y \) be positive integers. If for each positive integer \( n \) we have that

\[
(n y)^{2}+1 \mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1
\]

prove that \( x=1 \).
